Otamansha

A website for a countryside restaurant in Bucha, near Kyiv, with Ukrainian, European and Georgian cuisine. One site had to handle table booking, delivery, pickup, catering and the restaurant's own drive-through street food spot, and work first of all on a phone.

My role

A redesign, from research to final screens

I designed the website at Saphira Agency, working with our design team lead and a project manager. I did the research: I went through the restaurant's existing website, looked at competitors and read guest reviews. I also visited the restaurant to see the place and feel its atmosphere before designing anything.

Challenge

One restaurant, five ways to be a guest

The client wanted a redesign that would make the restaurant stronger online, make the site easier to use and bring more bookings and orders. The old site didn't show the place well, and it wasn't easy to find your way around it.

  1. 01

    Five services, one clear path

    A guest might want to book a table, order delivery, pick up food, plan a catered event or stop by the drive-through. Each of these needed an obvious way in, without turning the homepage into a list of everything.

  2. 02

    Most guests come from a phone

    According to the owners, most orders and bookings came from mobile phones. So I designed the mobile version first and built the desktop layout from it.

  3. 03

    It should feel like the place

    Otamansha is a cozy countryside restaurant with a green terrace. The site had to feel warm and welcoming, not like a generic delivery app.

Process

Mobile wireframes first, then desktop

After the research I reworked the information architecture: the menu structure was reorganized, and the restaurant's story and menu were placed where guests look for them. Then I wireframed the key mobile pages and made interactive prototypes to review the flows with the team and the owners. Desktop came after the mobile version was agreed.

Mobile wireframes
Desktop wireframes

Deep dive 01

Booking a table from the first screen

More bookings was one of the client's main goals, so booking is the first thing a guest can do on the site.

  1. 01

    A booking form inside the hero

    On desktop, the hero carries the whole booking form: name, phone, date, time and number of guests, plus one button. A guest can book without leaving the homepage or opening another page.

  2. 02

    A short form on mobile

    On a phone, the same fields open in a compact form from the "Book a table" button. After sending, the guest sees a confirmation that a manager will call back to confirm the booking.

  3. 03

    The offer repeats down the page

    Booking also appears after the restaurant's story and in a full-width banner further down, so a guest who scrolls to learn more doesn't have to go back up.

Desktop: booking in the hero
Mobile: booking form
Wireframe: form and confirmation

Deep dive 02

Ordering: delivery or pickup

Ordering food is the flow guests use most on their phones, so it got the most attention.

  1. 01

    A menu you can scan

    The menu has search and category chips at the top, and each dish card shows its weight, price and an "Add to cart" button on the photo itself.

  2. 02

    Two ways to get your order, side by side

    In the cart, "Pickup −15%" and "Delivery" sit next to each other. Each leads to a short form: time slots, payment method, a comment and the order summary. Delivery also asks for an address.

  3. 03

    A discount for pickup

    The 15% pickup discount was my idea. I proposed it at a meeting with the owners, and they took it on. It gives guests a reason to come and pick up their order themselves.

Visual direction

Wheat fields and fresh bread

After visiting the restaurant, I built the look around its warmth: the color of freshly baked goods, wheat fields and the thatched roofs of Ukrainian homesteads. The palette comes from the restaurant's food, with a dark graphite for contrast and a golden accent for actions. Proxima Nova keeps menus and forms easy to read.

Outcome

Handed over, never launched

The finished design was handed over to the owners, and they were very happy with it. The site never went live: soon after, Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
